candidates.attacker_control: Any unauthenticated network client controls the JWT it presents (cookie named by `server.session.state.jwt.name`, default "TOKEN", or a header when allowUseHeader=true) and can also set the session-id cookie (SessionProps.session_cookieName, default "SOLONID"). The signing key needed to produce a valid token is a compile-time constant that is published with the framework source (and the module README states the secret may be omitted and shows a sample secret, reinforcing that operators often leave it unset).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the default key can be overridden: `server.session.state.jwt.secret` takes precedence (JwtSessionStateFactory lines 38-43) and `signKeySet()` exists — but it is never invoked anywhere in the repository, the config default is empty/null, and the plugin does not require or warn about a secret. Checked claim-version/expiration handling: allowExpire only requires a future `exp`, which the attacker sets; the session-id equality check in cookie mode is satisfied by the attacker choosing both the session cookie and the token `jti` (values longer than 30 chars are accepted as-is). Checked that this is not a test-only artifact: the module is listed as published in V3.0.md (solon-sessionstate-jwt / solon.sessionstate.jwt) and is part of __release/solon-base-bundle3. Checked that no other key initialization path exists (`JwtUtils.getKey()` is the single verification/signing key source).
candidates.impact: Forgery of arbitrary session contents to any application that uses this plugin with default configuration: authentication bypass / user impersonation / privilege escalation where the session holds identity or authorization state, plus ability to set or tamper with any value the application stores in session. Because the key is a constant, the flaw is not limited to one installation; every default-configured deployment shares the public key.
candidates.prerequisites: The application includes the published `solon-sessionstate-jwt` artifact (it is part of the solon-base-bundle3 release bundle and of the documented plugin list) with session state enabled, uses the default configuration (no `server.session.state.jwt.secret`), and makes authentication/authorization decisions from values stored in the Solon session (a common pattern, e.g. user id / login flag kept in session).
candidates.root_cause: JwtSessionStateFactory keeps a constant HMAC-SHA256 key ("DHPjbM5QczZ2cysd4gpDbG/4SnuwzWX3sA1i6AXiAbo=") and only overrides it if `server.session.state.jwt.secret` is non-empty (JwtSessionProps.secret has no default). The plugin registers this factory as the application SessionStateFactory by default, and JwtUtils both verifies incoming tokens and signs outgoing tokens with exactly this key; no warning, no forced configuration, and `signKeySet()` is never called anywhere in the repository.
candidates.title: Hard-coded default JWT signing key in solon-sessionstate-jwt enables session/token forgery
candidates.trace: 1) SessionstateJwtPlugin.start() calls chainManager().setSessionStateFactory(JwtSessionStateFactory.getInstance()) unless a higher-priority factory is present. 2) JwtSessionStateFactory's constructor reads JwtSessionProps.secret; when config is absent it keeps the constant `signKey`. 3) JwtSessionState.sessionMap() reads the token via jwtGet() and calls JwtUtils.parseJwt(token); JwtUtils.getKey() derives the verification key from the same factory `signKey()` and parseJwt() calls Jwts.parserBuilder().setSigningKey(key)...parseClaimsJws(token) — so a token signed with the constant key verifies successfully. 4) If allowUseHeader is true, or the token's `jti` equals the attacker-chosen session cookie value (attacker supplies both cookies; `sessionIdGet` accepts any cookie value longer than 30 chars), the claims replace the session map. 5) sessionGet()/sessionOrDefault() then return attacker-chosen values (e.g. a chosen user id), and sessionPublish() re-signs with the same key (no key rotation or server-side revocation), so the forged session persists.
candidates.unverified: No build/test/runtime execution was performed; JJWT behavior (HS256 key derivation from the 32-byte Base64 constant) and the app-side impact were reasoned from source only. Whether a specific deployment sets `server.session.state.jwt.secret` and how heavily it relies on session contents were not observable from the snapshot. It was not determined whether this default predates or postdates nearby versions (no version history beyond UPDATE_LOG is available).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-321 Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key / CWE-1188 Insecure Default Initialization of Resource

coverage_summary: Tools used: get_source_scope (2,553 source files; binary files refused by read_file/search_code; no >5MiB exclusions reported) and get_relation_scope (index partial: 2,544 files indexed, 9 source files missing from the index, 2,080 Java files parsed, 23,942 unresolved calls, no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution). I inspected representative request-handling and security-relevant code across solon core (Context/path, RenderManager, PathMatcher/PathRule), solon-web (staticfiles incl. StaticMappings/File/ClassPath repositories, servlet adapters, webdav, cors, sdl, sessionstate-jwt/jedis), solon-boot (WebContextBase path decoding, OutputUtils, DecodeUtils, smarthttp/jdkhttp contexts and multipart handling), solon-serialization and nami coders (fury/hessian/jackson/fastjson), solon-net-httputils (HttpSsl, Jdk/OkHttp utils), solon-security (auth, validation, vault, web headers), solon-cloud-gateway, solon-data cache/javabin, solon-faas-luffy, solon-tool and the __hatch incubator modules, plus UPDATE_LOG/V3.0.md for shipped-vs-experimental context. This is a broad but non-exhaustive review; no build, test, scanner or exploit execution was performed and no runtime confirmation is claimed.
limitations: No build, tests or runtime checks were executed; all findings are source-based and could not be runtime-confirmed.

The relation index provides only syntactic navigation candidates: no data flow, control flow or semantic resolution, and 9 files are absent from the index; unreported areas cannot be claimed as reviewed.
Third-party dependency code (e.g. fastjson, jackson, fury, hessian, hutool, okhttp) is not in the snapshot, so verification relied on documented library semantics rather than source inspection.
Version/history is unavailable beyond in-repo changelogs, so it could not be determined whether the hard-coded default JWT key is long-standing or recently introduced.

The exact per-application impact of the JWT candidate depends on deployment configuration (whether a secret is set) and on how the application consumes session state; those factors are outside the snapshot.
Some modules are explicitly unpublished/experimental (__hatch, solon-web-webdav marked 略过（未发布）), so their issues have a weaker realistic attack surface.

rejected_leads.lead: WebDAV path traversal / arbitrary file read-write: WebdavAbstractHandler.stripPrefix() only URI-decodes and strips the configured prefix, and LocalFileSystem.realPath() concatenates rootPath + "/" + path with no normalization or containment check, so `../` in the request path reaches new File(...)/FileUtil.getInputStream(...) and PUT/DELETE/COPY/MOVE operate outside root.
rejected_leads.reason: Real defect, but the module is explicitly marked '略过（未发布）' (skipped/unpublished) in V3.0.md, requires an application-provided WebdavAbstractHandler implementation plus a non-blank user() result, so evidence of a reachable, shipped attack surface is weaker than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Fury deserialization used as an HTTP request-body deserializer while the class checker is configured with AllowListChecker.CheckLevel.WARN and requireClassRegistration(false) (FuryBytesSerializer/FuryActionExecutor, mirrored in nami-coder-fury/FuryUtil).
rejected_leads.reason: The blacklist is configured not to block (WARN only logs), which is a clear weakness, but exploitation needs the app to select the Fury serializer for request bodies and a usable gadget class on the classpath; no concrete gadget chain could be verified from source.

rejected_leads.lead: Hessian request-body deserialization with no class restriction (HessianBytesSerializer.deserializeFromBody -> Hessian2Input.readObject) and Jackson default typing enabled with the default permissive PolymorphicTypeValidator in JacksonActionExecutor/JacksonStringSerializer (plus nami-coder-jackson).
rejected_leads.reason: Both are deserialization-typed risks of the same class as the Fury lead; the Jackson '@type' behavior is an intentional framework feature (ContentTypes.AT_TYPE_JSON), and remote exploitation additionally requires endpoints binding bodies to Object-typed/generic parameters and a gadget on the classpath, so they were left as unconfirmed leads.

rejected_leads.lead: Nami FastjsonDecoder static block calls ParserConfig.getGlobalInstance().setAutoTypeSupport(true), globally enabling fastjson auto-type in the JVM (and Fastjson2Decoder parses with JSONReader.Feature.SupportAutoType).
rejected_leads.reason: A dangerous global security downgrade, but it becomes directly exploitable only through the application's own fastjson parsing of untrusted input or through attacker-influenced upstream responses; the decoder itself parses RPC results, so the direct remote path is not established from source.

rejected_leads.lead: Trust-all TLS in the built-in HTTP client: HttpSsl.DefaultX509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted() is empty and DefaultHostnameVerifier.verify() always returns true, and both JdkHttpUtils and OkHttpUtilsFactory apply them unconditionally to every HTTPS request (also used by nami-channel-http).
rejected_leads.reason: Strong code evidence of disabled certificate and hostname verification, but impact requires a man-in-the-middle network position against outbound HTTPS traffic from the app; direct attacker control of request/response content is weaker than the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: CORS defaults reflect any request Origin while emitting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (AbstractCross: allowedOrigins="*", allowCredentials=true, headerSet("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible cross-origin data-theft configuration weakness, but it is default behavior of an opt-in CORS plugin and the impact depends on cookie-based auth and endpoint responses; no direct authentication bypass is demonstrated from source.

summary: Source-level review of the assigned snapshot (Solon Java framework, version 3.1.3-SNAPSHOT; 2,553 source files, 2,544 indexed). I traced request-, configuration- and crypto-related flows across the published web, session, serialization, net/http, security and boot modules. The strongest, most concrete issue found is in the published `solon-sessionstate-jwt` plugin: it silently falls back to a hard-coded, publicly known HMAC-SHA256 signing key whenever `server.session.state.jwt.secret` is not configured, and the same key is used both to sign and to verify session JWTs. Because the plugin activates this factory by default (subject to session-state priority) and never warns or requires configuration, an unauthenticated remote client that knows the default key (it is in the public source, and the README even documents that the secret may be omitted) can mint a valid token whose claims become the request session — i.e. session/identity forgery and all application authorization decisions that rely on session values. Several other real but lower-ranked weaknesses were found and are listed as rejected leads (WebDAV path traversal; unenforced Fury blacklist with class registration disabled used for request bodies; Hessian/Jackson typed deserialization; global fastjson autoType; trust-all TLS in the built-in HTTP client; reflected-origin CORS with credentials by default). No runtime execution, build or test was performed; all statements are based on source text only.
